data.raw_text:
Big Corruption sits today in the Philippines, and the FLOOD CONTROL MESS has become the Poster Child: A Short Briefer on the Flood-Control Corruption in the Philippines (as of 12 Sep 2025). Note: This is NOT Exhaustive! This is just the surface!

The Big and Broad Picture: Corruption Remains Systemic!

 Perception Index: In the 2024 Transparency International CPI, the Philippines scored 33/100 and ranked 114th of 180, slipping one point from 2023—still a sign of persistent governance risk. 

 Where it Bites Most?: Public procurement and infrastructure are perennial hotspots; research estimates corruption can add 10–25% to contract costs when safeguards fail (kickbacks, bid‑rigging, collusion). 

 Legal Framework: Procurement is governed by the New Government Procurement Act (RA 12009, 2024)—which superseded RA 9184—and its 2025 IRR. The law now embeds open data, beneficial-ownership disclosure, and stronger observation and recording of bid proceedings through PhilGEPS to curb abuse; its effectiveness depends on implementation. 

What’s Going On? 

 Budget Scale and Fragmentation: The private sector notes that DPWH’s budget growth is “disproportionate” and that flood control now accounts for about one-third of infrastructure outlays, receiving over ₱1.2 trillion from 2023 to 2026 (₱250B proposed for 2026). Small, repetitive line items (ripraps, river walls, desilting) are easy to insert, repeat, and disguise. BusinessWorld

 Insertions/earmarks dynamics: Alleged “congressional insertions” into flood control line items have been flagged in hearings and reportage, recently citing a ₱355M insertion cluster and linking some 2025 items to “insertions” paths. (These are allegations; probes are active.) Inquirer.net+1

• Televised House/Senate probes heard sworn claims of 25–30% “commissions” on flood-control contracts; 17 House members and later two senators were named—all deny wrongdoing. The scandal triggered the DPWH secretary’s resignation and the creation of an independent commission to build cases. AP News+2AP News+2

• New DPWH chief Vince Dizon has paused bidding for all locally funded DPWH projects, demanded courtesy resignations, and filed the first criminal complaints (20 personnel + 4 contractors) over Bulacan flood works. GMA Network+1

• COA has transmitted fraud-audit reports on Bulacan “ghost/substandard” projects to the Ombudsman, and disclosed a decade-long trail of P308 B in questioned DPWH disbursements (notices of suspension/disallowance/charge). Inquirer News+1

• Malacañang and the Senate both flagged market concentration: 15 contractors reportedly cornered ~20% of ~P545 B flood funds since 2022. Philstar

• The 2024 Corruption Perceptions Index scores the Philippines 33/100 (rank 114/180)—persistent governance risk. https://t.co/3cFSLkknu7

Do you know what's IMPACT?:

• Lives & Livelihoods: Substandard or phantom work exacerbates flooding and undermines the credibility of risk reduction—amid stronger typhoons. This is not just a corruption issue; this is also a humanitarian issue that the public must be outraged about! 

• Budget Credibility & Growth: Wasted capex crowds out social spending and undermines investor confidence.

• ODA vs. Local Funds: Foreign-assisted projects will definitely and should have tighter oversight, while locally funded packages are under the harshest scrutiny now, potentially leading to more bidding suspensions, cancellations, and, in the worst-case scenario, filings. 

• The country is CONTINUOUSLY ROTTING, SINKING, and in CONFLAGRATION! Goodness! 

So what now, folks??? 
Anong ang sigaw ng bayan?
Anong sigaw ng mamayang Pilipino???
Let your voice be heard, Filipino compatriots!!!

#exposethedeception
#ExposeTheTruth
#ProPhilippines
